hero.headline: Jupiter Island faces up to 9 feet of flooding at emergency center, leaders say they're prepared
hero.body:
Jupiter Island's Emergency Operations Center could see up to 9 feet of floodwater during future storms, according to a new vulnerability assessment by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The report identified 103 critical town assets at risk of flooding, including 68 stormwater facilities, 17 historic sites, conservation lands, and key evacuation routes.

Commissioner Marshall Field told reporters the findings confirm what town leaders already knew when they requested the assessment. The town's Beach District Director John Duchok said the assessment will set up a roadmap for how to adapt and prioritize improvements. Field said the goal is to document the risks, build a roadmap for improvements, and compete for state and federal funding to fix vulnerabilities.

Field addressed immediate concerns about the island's vulnerability, saying evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways. The town has a backup facility on the mainland to maintain operations during emergencies. The 126-page report warns that stormwater systems face some of the greatest risks, noting they can fail during the very flooding events they are designed to manage. Field said there is a funding window that opened June 1 for applications, and the town will take advantage of it.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an illegal medical spa from a shed in her Port St. Lucie backyard. Police began investigating after a victim came forward in May 2025 reporting partial facial paralysis following services at Mena's business, Miracle Hand and Spa, located at the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive.

The victim received 62 units of Botox injections during a session at the makeshift med spa. When the paralysis developed, Mena refunded the $325 fee and asked the victim to return for vitamin injections to reverse the issues. After the paralysis persisted, the victim requested Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that had expired in February 2024. Mena also claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation by Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox. Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges, and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony.

cards.headline: Florida TaxWatch criticizes rushed property tax cut proposal ahead of special session
cards.body:
Florida TaxWatch, an influential government watchdog organization that has monitored state taxation and spending for 47 years, released a sharp analysis warning against Gov. Ron DeSantis's property tax cut proposal being decided in a special session. The organization called for the issue to be taken up instead by the Taxation and Budget Reform Commission, a constitutionally mandated group that Florida TaxWatch helped establish.

The analysis examined DeSantis's proposal to increase the state's homestead exemption from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027, then to $250,000 in 2028. While Florida TaxWatch praised the conversation about lowering property taxes and agreed that significant relief is warranted, the report warned that the government cannot solve affordability by simply addressing property tax increases. The organization noted that guardrails are needed to curb local government spending, which it said has far exceeded the growth in population and inflation over the last 10 years.

The TaxWatch analysis drew criticism from former lawmaker Bob Rommel, Florida State Chair of the America First Policy Institute, who questioned on social media where the organization had been for the last seven years while local government spending increased 300 percent above inflation. The analysis itself pointed to Florida TaxWatch's ongoing work on ensuring state and local governments are good stewards of taxpayer dollars, including a report titled Save Our Taxpayers that called for property tax relief to be accomplished equitably.

Billed as an independent and nonpartisan research institute, Florida TaxWatch is often considered a conservative think tank because of its hard-line approach to taxation. The organization regularly produces a list of budget turkeys cautioning against government spending excess and provides information to residents and public officials about local government taxation, expenditures, policies and programs.

Jupiter Island Commissioner Marshall Field said the findings confirm what town leaders already knew when they requested the assessment. Field and Beach District Director John Duchok explained the study will create a roadmap for improvements, with town leaders planning to apply for state and federal funding starting June 1. The 126-page report warns that stormwater systems face some of the greatest risks because they can fail during the very flooding events they are designed to manage.

The findings come after a separate state study warned that severe erosion could one day break through part of the island. Field said evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways, and that the town has a backup facility on the mainland to maintain operations during emergencies. The town is embedded with the county's emergency response system. Field acknowledged that drainage improvements are challenging on the narrow island, where conventional stormwater management approaches used on the mainland don't work the same way.

cards.headline: Florida lawmakers pass property tax cut proposal requiring voter approval
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000, but voters must approve it in November.
cards.body:
Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut proposal on Tuesday that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The measure would lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10% to 5%. The proposal requires approval from 60% of voters in November before taking effect.

Experts offered varying perspectives on potential consequences. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace noted possible new non-ad valorem taxes for services like the sheriff's office and fire rescue. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could face increased fees to offset lost county revenue. Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi predicted home prices could increase, while MIAMI REALTORS + RWorld Chief Danielle Blake cited interest rates as a more significant barrier to sales than property taxes.

cards.teaser: Jupiter dedicated Fire Station 10 on U.S. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park as the town prepares to take over its own fire rescue service this fall.
cards.body:
Jupiter has opened Fire Station 10, marking a historic milestone as the town prepares to assume control of its own fire rescue service this fall. The new station, located on U.S. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park, held a dedication ceremony attended by firefighters, town leaders and community members.

The event celebrated a tradition rooted in more than a century of history, described as "the uncoupling." This transition represents a significant shift in how Jupiter will manage its emergency fire and rescue operations going forward.

hero.teaser: Crews began tearing down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a revitalization project that will transform the site into a modern indoor and outdoor shopping center.
hero.body:
Demolition crews began work this week on the Indian River Mall, starting with the Macy's building and the former Sears location. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said the effort is the first phase of a revitalization project for the shopping center.

The site will be transformed into a mixed-use indoor and outdoor shopping center with approximately 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants, and possible residential spaces. Scarfone said the first phase is expected to be completed by 2027, though the team is still working on permitting for the remainder of the project.

The Emergency Operations Center could see up to 9 feet of floodwater, according to the report.

Commissioner Marshall Field said the findings confirm what town leaders already knew, which is why they requested the assessment. Field said evacuation orders would be issued well before floodwaters threaten roadways, and the town has a backup facility on the mainland to maintain operations during emergencies. The town plans to apply for state and federal funding to address vulnerabilities.

cards.headline: 12 Make-A-Wish kids sworn in as junior deputies at St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office
cards.teaser: Sheriff Richard Del Toro honored 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation by swearing them in as junior deputies and giving them a full tour of law enforcement operations.
cards.body:
Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro at the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office on Wednesday. The young honorees received badges, toured the facility, and witnessed K-9 demonstrations, a SWAT team presentation, and a helicopter display.

Among the new deputies were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia in 2023 and required a bone marrow transplant that her twin brother provided. Also sworn in was Tobias, who was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022 and recovered after critical medical intervention. Sheriff Del Toro said the children "made our wish come true."

cards.headline: 80-mile ocean paddle race to finish at Lake Worth Beach for cystic fibrosis fundraiser
cards.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross open ocean from the Bahamas to raise money for families living with cystic fibrosis.
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean this June in the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Participants launch from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours of paddling. Event founder Travis Suit created the endurance trek to benefit the Piper's Angels Foundation, established in honor of his daughter Piper, diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times. Participants must raise at least $2,000, with a $500 minimum for crew or virtual participants. Contributions are due July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong celebration.

cards.headline: 'Beetlejuice' the musical brings Broadway to West Palm Beach's Kravis Center through June 7
cards.teaser: The Broadway hit runs at the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall with performances through this weekend.
cards.body:
The musical "Beetlejuice" runs at the Kravis Center's Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall from June 2 through June 7. Actor Ryan Stajmiger plays the mischievous demon in the striped suit, a role Michael Keaton made iconic in Tim Burton's 1988 film. The production features the story of Lydia Deetz, a teen whose life changes after meeting two deceased neighbors and a troublemaking demon.

Stajmiger highlighted his favorite aspect of performing: breaking the fourth wall to communicate directly with audiences. During an early performance, a wig change went unexpectedly awry when both wigs came off together, leaving him bald for an entire scene. Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows June 3-4, 8 p.m. June 5, matinee and evening shows June 6, and a closing matinee June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after running an illegal med spa out of a shed in her Port St. Lucie backyard. A victim came to police in May 2025 reporting partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections at a makeshift med spa inside the backyard shed called Miracle Hand and Spa. The victim had been referred to the business by coworkers who had received services from Mena in the past.

After the victim reported the paralysis to Mena, Mena refunded the $325 paid for the services and asked the victim to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the issues. When the paralysis persisted, the victim requested to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered certificate of phlebotomy that had expired in February 2024. Mena also told the victim she was a doctor from the Dominican Republic in an attempt to ease concerns.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, the PSL Business Tax and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines and injection devices for fillers and Botox. Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony.

hero.headline: Indian River Mall demolition underway in Vero Beach as mixed-use redevelopment begins
hero.body:
Crews began taking down portions of the Indian River Mall this week as part of a major revitalization project for the longtime shopping center. Project manager Joseph Scarfone said work is focused on the first phase, which involves demolishing the Macy's building and the former Sears location.

Neighbors gathered in the mall parking lot to watch the demolition. Mary Alice Stopyra said she's happy to see the structure come down after years of decline. Mark Manera, a Vero Beach resident who has visited the mall for years, described it as looking like a graveyard in recent times. Manera said he watched a steady decline year after year and believes change is needed. He hopes the project will bring new life, new jobs and new opportunities to the area.

Scarfone said the site will be transformed into a sleek and modern indoor and outdoor shopping center with around 300,000 square feet of retail, restaurants and possible residential spaces. He called it a city within a city, noting that residents won't see a dead mall that's been collecting cobwebs for the last 12 years. The project manager hopes the first phase can be completed by 2027, and crews are still working on permitting for the rest of the project.
